stories.headline: NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG RESIGNS AS BOARD NAMES CFO KRESS INTERIM CHIEF AFTER ESPIONAGE SCANDAL
stories.body: Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO and director effective immediately, per an 8-K filed late Wednesday, naming CFO Colette Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor and elevating longtime director Harvey Jones to the company's first-ever board-chair role. The move follows a board probe into reports that Huang carried on a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was gathering information for Beijing, and lawmakers have reportedly asked Huang to brief Congress as soon as next week.
stories.explain: A CEO exit at a company this size is priced less as a one-day headline than as a change to the discount rate applied to the entire franchise: investors now have to underwrite execution risk under interim leadership plus the odds that a drawn-out succession search or congressional scrutiny distracts from Nvidia's roadmap. Because Nvidia carries one of the largest single weights in both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, that repricing mechanically drags both cap-weighted indices even though nothing changed about AI chip demand itself.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS 0.33%, NASDAQ 100 OFF 0.30% AS NVIDIA SHAKE-UP MEETS RISING YIELDS
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.33% to 7,592 and the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.30% to 28,289 as Nvidia's leadership upheaval compounded a 10-basis-point rise in the benchmark yield to 5.10%, a one-two punch of idiosyncratic and macro pressure on growth stocks. The decline followed Wednesday's rally and left most sectors lower on the session.
stories.explain: Growth and AI-infrastructure names carry long-duration cash-flow profiles, so they get hit twice when yields rise at the same time a bellwether's governance is in flux: the discount rate on those future earnings goes up mechanically, and the earnings estimate itself becomes less certain. That combination, rather than either factor alone, is what turned a one-stock governance story into a broad index move today.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS HOLD NEAR 82-85% UNDER WARSH AS YIELDS PUSH TOWARD 5.10%
stories.body: Fed funds futures continue to price roughly an 82-85% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting under Chair Kevin Warsh, with the benchmark yield climbing 10 bps to 5.10% today as that pricing held firm alongside the Nvidia-driven equity selloff.
stories.explain: Rate-hike odds this elevated function as a floor under yields: as long as the market keeps pricing a near-certain hike, the 10-year has little room to rally even on a risk-off day, which is why yields rose rather than fell despite equities selling off. That combination of higher yields and falling stocks is the textbook signature of a rate-driven repricing rather than a flight-to-safety bid, and it raises the stakes for Friday's PPI print as the next data point that could move those odds.

stories.headline: OCTOBER PPI DUE FRIDAY WILL TEST WHETHER TUESDAY'S HOT CORE CPI IS CONFIRMED UPSTREAM
stories.body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases October producer prices Friday at 8:30 AM ET, the next data point the Fed will weigh before its Dec. 8-9 meeting after this week's hotter-than-expected core CPI reading helped push hike odds into the 82-85% range.
stories.explain: PPI measures price pressure at the wholesale and input level before it reaches consumers, so a hot reading tends to be read as confirmation that CPI's firmness has supply-chain roots rather than being a one-off, while a soft print would give the Fed room to argue December's hike case is less clear-cut. Because PPI also feeds into the core PCE calculation the Fed actually targets, Friday's number carries more weight for the December decision than its modest market billing suggests.

stories.headline: GOLD DROPS 2.5% AS REAL YIELDS RISE; WTI JUMPS 4% AS OIL DECOUPLES FROM THE RISK-OFF TAPE
stories.body: Gold fell 2.48% to $3,882 an ounce as the yield rise lifted the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, while the DXY dollar index firmed 0.19% to 103.19; WTI crude bucked the broader risk-off mood, jumping 4.02% to $89 a barrel on supply-side concerns distinct from today's equity and rate story.
stories.explain: Gold's decline is the direct mirror image of today's yield move: every basis point added to the real rate raises the cost of holding a zero-yield asset, and a firming dollar compounds that by making gold pricier for non-dollar buyers. Oil's rally despite the same hawkish, risk-off backdrop shows crude traders are pricing a supply-specific catalyst rather than reacting to equities or rates, which is why it moved opposite to gold and stocks on the same day.

watchlist: October PPI due Friday, Nov. 13 at 8:30 AM ET — will show whether CPI's hot core reading is confirmed further upstream in the supply chain

deepDive.title: Key-Person Risk and Index Concentration: What Nvidia's CEO Shock Reveals About Cap-Weighted Markets
content: Today's selloff was led by a single governance event: Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO following a probe into his ties to an alleged foreign-intelligence operative, naming CFO Colette Kress interim chief. The S&P 500 fell 0.33% and the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.30% on a day when nothing changed about AI chip demand, supply chains, or earnings power. The reason one company's leadership shake-up moved two broad indices is mechanical, and it is a feature every student of cap-weighted benchmarks needs to understand before trusting an index-level number to tell them what actually happened in the economy that day.

Cap-weighted indices like the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 assign each constituent a weight proportional to its market capitalization, so a stock carrying roughly 6-8% of the index moves the whole benchmark by a fraction of its own percentage move, no vote or aggregation required. When Nvidia's price falls on leadership uncertainty, that decline is multiplied by its weight and summed directly into the index level, the same arithmetic that makes an index gain or lose points. This is why today's headline 'the market fell' is really shorthand for 'one of the market's largest holdings fell,' and why index-level moves can overstate how broadly a shock is actually felt across the economy.

What's easy to miss is that key-person risk itself carries a market price, distinct from the earnings risk analysts usually model. Apple's stock has swung on Tim Cook succession chatter, Tesla trades partly on Elon Musk's attention, and Berkshire Hathaway carried a long-discussed 'Buffett discount' tied to eventual succession; in each case, the market priced not the company's cash flows directly but the uncertainty around who controls the decisions that produce them. Boeing's 2019 leadership turnover amid the 737 MAX crisis is the closer parallel: the stock kept falling even as technical fixes progressed, because the market was pricing governance and execution risk, not just the grounded fleet.

For the next few weeks, this mechanism matters more than usual because Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 earnings on Nov. 17, the first major test of whether Kress can hold investor confidence as interim CEO while a permanent search plays out, possibly alongside a congressional briefing on the espionage allegations. A clean print that reassures the market on demand and execution would let Nvidia's weight stop acting as a drag on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100; a messy one, compounded by the still-elevated odds of a December Fed hike, would mean concentration risk keeps doing double duty as both a company story and a market-wide one.
